XVI.1.title: Trouble within the screen
XVI.1.reflection: The Ji family plans to attack the small dependency of Zhuanyu, and Ran Qiu and Zilu, who serve the Ji, report it. Confucius blames Ran Qiu: if an adviser cannot steady his master, what use is he? When a tiger escapes, whose fault is it? Ran Qiu argues the town is a future threat; the junzi hates those who will not say "I want it" and invent reasons instead. A state should worry less about too few people or too little wealth than about unequal shares and unrest. The Ji family's real trouble, he ends, lies within its own walls.
XVI.1.question: What have you wanted while explaining that you had other reasons?

XVI.2.title: Ten, five, three generations
XVI.2.reflection: When the world has the Way, ritual, music and war come from the Son of Heaven; when it does not, from the lords, and they seldom last ten generations; from their ministers, five; from the ministers' stewards, three. When the Way prevails, the common people do not debate government. Power taken from above drains away faster the lower it settles.
XVI.2.question: Where have you seen authority taken by those it did not belong to, and how long did it last?

XVI.3.title: Five generations
XVI.3.reflection: For five generations the revenue has left the ducal house; for four the great officers have held the government; so the descendants of the three Huan families, who seized it, are now in decline themselves. The previous chapter's rule, applied to Lu.
XVI.3.question: What gain have you seen undone by the same means it was won?

XVI.4.title: Three friends who help
XVI.4.reflection: Three kinds of friend help: the upright, the trustworthy, the well-informed. Three harm: the flatterer, the one who is all soft compliance, the glib talker. Book XVI likes lists of three, which suggests a different source from the earlier books.
XVI.4.question: Which of the six kinds of friend are you to others?

XVI.5.title: Three pleasures that help
XVI.5.reflection: Helpful pleasures: in the measure of ritual and music, in speaking of others' good, in many worthy friends. Harmful pleasures: in extravagance, in idle wandering, in feasting. What one enjoys shapes who one becomes.
XVI.5.question: Which of your pleasures do you hope will shape you?

XVI.6.title: Three errors before a superior
XVI.6.reflection: With a person of standing, there are three faults: speaking before it is your turn, which is rashness; not speaking when it is, which is concealment; speaking without watching their face, which is blindness. Good conversation is timing and attention.
XVI.6.question: Which of the three is your habit?

XVI.7.title: Three cautions through life
XVI.7.reflection: In youth, when the blood is unsettled, guard against lust; in maturity, when the blood is strong, guard against quarrelling; in old age, when the blood has weakened, guard against greed. Each age has its own temptation.
XVI.7.question: Which of the three belongs to your age now?

XVI.8.title: Three things in awe
XVI.8.reflection: The junzi stands in awe of Heaven's decree, of great men, and of the words of the sages. The small man does not know Heaven's decree, takes liberties with great men and mocks the sages' words. Awe is a form of knowledge here.
XVI.8.question: What do you still hold in awe?

XVI.9.title: Four kinds of learner
XVI.9.reflection: Born knowing, the highest; learning and so knowing, next; learning in difficulty, next; in difficulty and not learning, the lowest. In VII.19 Confucius placed himself in the second rank. The lowest are not the slow, but those who stop trying.
XVI.9.question: In what subject are you in the third rank, still learning in difficulty?

XVI.10.title: Nine things to think of
XVI.10.reflection: The junzi thinks of nine things: seeing clearly, hearing well, a gentle face, a respectful manner, loyal speech, serious work, asking when in doubt, the consequences when angry, and rightness when there is gain. A checklist for a whole day.
XVI.10.question: Which of the nine did you think of least today?
XVI.10.exercise: At one moment of anger today, pause and think of the consequences, as the ninth line asks.

XVI.11.title: Heard of, not seen
XVI.11.reflection: Seeing good and reaching for it as if one might miss it, seeing evil and pulling back as from boiling water: I have seen such people and heard such words. Living in retirement to pursue one's aim and practising rightness to reach one's Way: I have heard the words but not seen the people. The second is rarer.
XVI.11.question: What ideal have you heard of but never seen lived?

XVI.12.title: A thousand teams of horses
XVI.12.reflection: Duke Jing of Qi had a thousand teams of horses, and on the day he died the people found no virtue to praise. Bo Yi and Shu Qi starved beneath Mount Shouyang, and people praise them still. The chapter seems to have lost a line, the saying it says is illustrated.
XVI.12.question: What will people find to praise in you when you are gone?

XVI.13.title: The son and the father
XVI.13.reflection: Chen Kang asks Confucius's son, Boyu, whether he received special teaching. Only twice, passing his father in the courtyard: have you studied the Odes? If not, you will have nothing to say; have you studied ritual? If not, you will have nothing to stand on. Chen Kang leaves delighted to have learned three things: the Odes, ritual, and that the junzi keeps a distance from his son. The father taught his son as he taught everyone.
XVI.13.question: What did your parents teach you in passing that you still remember?

XVI.14.title: What a ruler's wife is called
XVI.14.reflection: The ruler calls his wife furen, she calls herself xiaotong, the people call her junfuren and so on. A chapter of terms of address, perhaps from a ritual handbook. It belongs to the book's concern with names matching roles, though it reads as a stray note.
XVI.14.question: How many different names do you go by in different places?
